C005.subject: Free trade policies combined with targeted retraining programs
C005.object: short-term job displacement duration by 40-60% in textile and agricultural sectors of developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies combined with targeted retraining programs short-term job displacement duration by 40-60% in textile and agricultural sectors of developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from Bangladesh's Ready-Made Garment (RMG) sector post-2004 MFA phase-out, combined with retraining program enrollment records from the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and government labor surveys — This would provide direct causal evidence of how trade liberalization and retraining affect re-employment speed in a developing economy's textile sector, allowing estimation of displacement duration reduction within 18 months.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental difference-in-differences analysis of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) Transitional Adjustment Assistance (TAA) program for displaced agricultural workers in Mexico, using Encuesta Nacional de Ocupación y Empleo (ENOE) microdata — This can isolate the effect of targeted retraining on job displacement duration by comparing treated workers (TAA recipients) to non-recipients in the same trade-affected agricultural regions, controlling for observable confounders.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on retraining programs in developing economies (e.g., J-PAL studies in India, Colombia) combined with trade shock exposure indices — Synthesizing evidence from multiple RCTs allows testing whether the hypothesized 40-60% reduction is consistent across contexts, and identifies moderators such as program design or sector-specific labor mobility.

C006.subject: Free trade policies
C006.object: rapid job creation in developing economies through export sector expansion that absorbs displaced workers within 12-18 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies rapid job creation in developing economies through export sector expansion that absorbs displaced workers within 12-18 months]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Enterprise Surveys and labor force panel data for East Asian and Latin American economies (1995-2015), focusing on export-oriented manufacturing sectors and tracking worker reallocation timelines — Directly tests the temporal absorption claim (12-18 months) by measuring job creation rates in export sectors and the duration of unemployment for displaced workers in the specified geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of trade liberalization episodes in South Korea (post-1997) and Mexico (post-NAFTA) using administrative employment records and firm-level export data — Provides within-country longitudinal evidence on whether export sector expansion actually absorbs displaced workers within the claimed timeframe, controlling for institutional differences across East Asia and Latin America.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of 20+ studies on the labor market effects of free trade agreements in developing economies, focusing on displacement duration and export sector job multipliers — Synthesizes existing empirical findings to assess the generalizability of the 12-18 month absorption claim, identifying conditions under which it holds or fails (e.g., skill mismatches, labor market rigidities).

qualifier.geographic: in developing economies in East Asia and Latin America

C007.subject: Pre-liberalization investment in worker retraining programs
C007.object: short-term job displacement from free trade policies by 40-60% in manufacturing sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Pre-liberalization investment in worker retraining programs short-term job displacement from free trade policies by 40-60% in manufacturing sectors]

[PATH:empirical] Country-level panel data on trade liberalization episodes (e.g., from the World Bank's Trade, Production, and Protection database) matched with administrative records on worker retraining program uptake and employment outcomes in textile/apparel sectors in low-income economies (e.g., Bangladesh, Vietnam, Ethiopia). — This quasi-experimental design can test the causal effect of pre-liberalization retraining on short-term job displacement by comparing sectors with and without such programs, controlling for pre-existing trends.

[PATH:empirical] Evaluations of specific retraining programs implemented before trade reforms, such as those by the International Labour Organization (ILO) or national ministries of labor in countries like Cambodia or Lesotho, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or difference-in-differences analyses. — These micro-level studies provide direct evidence on the magnitude of displacement reduction (40-60%) and identify mechanisms (e.g., skill transferability, job search assistance) that could confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Computable general equilibrium (CGE) models or dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models calibrated to low-income developing economies, incorporating worker retraining as a policy variable and simulating trade liberalization scenarios. — These models can test the theoretical plausibility of the claimed 40-60% reduction by simulating counterfactual labor market adjustments under different retraining intensities and timeframes, helping to assess whether the effect size is consistent with economic theory.

qualifier.temporal: when implemented 12-18 months before trade liberalization
qualifier.sectoral: textile, apparel, and light manufacturing industries

C008.subject: Free trade policies
C008.object: rapid job creation in export-oriented sectors that absorbs displaced workers within 6-12 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies rapid job creation in export-oriented sectors that absorbs displaced workers within 6-12 months]

[PATH:empirical] Country-level labor force surveys and firm-level export data from low-income developing economies (e.g., Bangladesh, Vietnam) covering the first 1-3 years after trade liberalization episodes — Directly tests the hypothesis by tracking sectoral employment reallocation and the time-to-reemployment for displaced workers, using difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity designs to isolate the effect of free trade policies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on trade liberalization and labor market adjustment in low-income countries with limited social safety nets — Synthesizes findings from multiple empirical papers (e.g., by Topalova, Goldberg & Pavcnik, and McCaig) to assess the consistency and magnitude of job absorption rates in export-oriented sectors, and to identify conditions under which the 6-12 month timeline holds or fails.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic general equilibrium model calibrated to a representative low-income developing economy, incorporating frictional labor markets and sectoral linkages — Provides a controlled simulation environment to explore the mechanisms and necessary conditions (e.g., wage flexibility, skill transferability, credit constraints) for rapid job creation and worker absorption, helping to bound the plausibility of the hypothesis when empirical data are scarce.

qualifier.temporal: during the initial post-liberalization period (1-3 years)
qualifier.geographic: in low-income developing economies with limited social safety nets

C009.subject: Free trade policies combined with strong domestic intellectual property enforcement
C009.object: high-value manufacturing capability development more than trade liberalization alone
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies combined with strong domestic intellectual property enforcement high-value manufacturing capability development more than trade liberalization alone]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of South Korea (strong IP enforcement) vs. Indonesia (weak IP enforcement) under similar free trade regimes, using patent and export data for high-value manufacturing sectors (e.g., electronics, pharmaceuticals) from 2000-2020. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing outcomes in middle-income East Asian economies with differing IP enforcement levels, controlling for trade liberalization.

[PATH:empirical] Econometric analysis of firm-level panel data from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys for middle-income East Asian economies, examining the interaction effect of free trade agreement participation and IP protection indices on firms' R&D investment and high-value product upgrades. — Provides statistical evidence on whether the combination of trade liberalization and strong IP enforcement yields a synergistic effect on capability development beyond trade alone.

qualifier.comparison: relative to economies with weak IP enforcement

C010.subject: Free trade policies
C010.object: long-term technological transfer and productivity growth for developing economies by preventing infant industry protection and locking them into low-value commodity production
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies long-term technological transfer and productivity growth for developing economies by preventing infant industry protection and locking them into low-value commodity production]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of manufacturing productivity and export complexity in Latin America and Sub-Saharan Africa (1990–2020) using UNIDO and World Bank trade liberalization indices — Directly tests whether periods of free trade policy adoption correlate with declining technological transfer (measured by total factor productivity growth) and shifts toward low-value commodity exports, controlling for other factors like human capital and infrastructure.

[PATH:literature] Case studies of infant industry protection in successful East Asian economies (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan) compared with liberalized sectors in Latin America (e.g., Mexico's maquiladoras) from the literature on 'premature deindustrialization' (e.g., Dani Rodrik, 2016; Ha-Joon Chang, 2002) — Provides qualitative and comparative evidence on the mechanism—whether the absence of protection under free trade leads to lock-in effects, while protected industries historically fostered technological upgrading and productivity growth.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model simulating dynamic comparative advantage and learning-by-doing under free trade vs. infant industry protection, calibrated to Sub-Saharan African parameters — Clarifies causal mechanisms: tests whether free trade consistently prevents technological transfer and locks economies into low-value production under plausible assumptions about learning rates, market failures, and spillovers.

qualifier.geographic: Latin American and Sub-Saharan African developing economies
